text:
An outcry is growing over the UK chancellor’s removal of most brownfield housing plots from a legal requirement for developers to measurably enhance nature.
John Healey’s decision in the budget to exempt brownfield plots of up to 1.5 hectares from biodiversity net gain (BNG) laws effectively means housing developers of inner-city, urban and surburban sites will be able to dodge rules designed to reverse steep wildlife declines while also allowing housebuilding growth. According to government data, 86% of brownfield sites currently registered are 1.5ha or under.
The Labour government has repeatedly chipped away at biodiversity net gain (BNG) rules, which make it mandatory for developers to improve nature by at least 10% when building projects.
The BNG law was seen as world-leading when introduced by the Conservatives in 2024, and has brought more than £320m of private investment into nature recovery, according to some estimates.
Healey’s brownfield exemption comes after Keir Starmer’s government rolled back the policy with exemptions that included the removal of all small sites of under 0.2 hectares. Taken together, the policy regression risks removing the vast majority of eligible development from any mandatory obligation to enhance nature, according to an assessment by the Chartered Institute of Ecology and Environmental management (CIEEM).
Sally Hayns, the chief executive of CIEEM, said: “We strongly oppose the introduction of an area-based exemption from biodiversity net gain on residential brownfield sites.
“CIEEM is particularly concerned that the 1.5ha exemption announced in the budget, together with existing exemptions introduced this year, could remove over 80% of all planning applications from BNG requirements. This would be inconsistent with government commitments that ‘most development’ should contribute to nature recovery.”
Brownfield sites include former retail areas in town centres, abandoned factories and redundant commercial buildings.
The rollback on the policy comes after intensive lobbying by housebuilders, and in the midst of catastrophic wildlife and habitat losses in the UK that rank it among the worst countries in the world for nature decline.
But the exemption is not yet in force and there is a marked pushback by environmental NGOs and some building organisations for it to be reconsidered.
Ministers are required to publish the results of a consultation on exempting brownfield sites – which ended in June – and to explain how the responses informed Healey’s policy decision. They have yet to do so.
If the government cannot justify its policy decision in the light of the consultation responses it could lead to a judicial review challenge.
Wildlife and Countryside Link, an umbrella group for about 80 environmental charities, said it strongly opposed the introduction of any new brownfield exemption from BNG in any form.
“We are deeply concerned that the proposals … alongside existing … exemptions, represent a cumulative and structural retreat from the core purpose and intended scope of BNG.”
The Wildlife Trusts said the chancellor’s decision risked disproportionately reducing opportunities to bring nature back into urban communities.
“Exempting brownfield developments from biodiversity net gain reduces access to nature in the communities that need it the most, and will remove one of the biggest opportunities to bring trees, ponds, wildlife and parks back into towns and cities,” said Dom Higgins, head of health and education at the Wildlife Trusts.
“Access to nature should not be a luxury. We know that designing housing and infrastructure with trees, parks and space for nature is proven to improve mental and physical health and boost people’s pride in their communities. These habitats also provide vital shade and cooling effects during heatwaves, along with helping to reduce the risk of flooding.”
The UK Green Building Council said it opposed exempting sites solely because they were brownfield in planning terms rather than because they were demonstrably low in biodiversity value.
Claire Traynor, chief commercial officer at Nattergal, a UK-based nature restoration and rewilding company, said the exemptions struck at the heart of a globally recognised market that was on track to deliver hundreds of millions of pounds of private investment into nature recovery before the next election.
“The government cannot continue to use exemptions on nature to wallpaper over much deeper cracks in the planning and development sectors,” she said. “Successive policy changes erode investor confidence and send the message that the UK is not serious about creating the stable financial markets needed to unlock long-term private investment and support sustainable economic growth.”
The latest rollback of the biodiversity enhancement rules by Healey is being seen as another blow to nature enhancement by a government that is failing to progress its international commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature’s recovery by 2030.
BNG became mandatory for nationally significant infrastructure projects (NSIPs) this month, as the brownfield exemptions were announced.
A government spokesperson said: “This government is making the largest investment into nature in history, with over £7bn directed into nature’s recovery so biodiversity can thrive.
“Biodiversity net gain is a world-leading nature and development policy that allows development to go ahead while enhancing our natural environment – and we have always been clear it must operate proportionally. This country desperately needs more homes to be built, and brownfield land should be the first port of call for development.”
digest_he:
גל של ביקורת ציבורית נרשם בבריטניה בעקבות החלטת שר האוצר פטור את רוב אתרי הבנייה העירוניים מן הדרישה החוקית לחייב יזמים לשפר באופן מדיד את הסביבה הטבעית. לפי הנתונים הממשלתיים, 86 אחוזים מהאתרים הרשומים כיום הם בשטח של עד 1.5 דונם, כך שההחלטה צפויה להסיר את רוב בקשות הבנייה מחובת שיפור הביו-דיברסיטי בשיעור של לפחות 10 אחוזים.

ארגוני סביבה וגופים מקצועיים הזהירו כי המהלך יחמיר את משבר הטבע החמור שבו מצויה בריטניה ויפגע בנגישות הציבור שטבע עירוני. לטענת המבקרים, הפטור החדש מצטרף לשורת הקלות רגולטוריות המכרסמות במדיניות הסביבתית ופוגעות באמון המשקיעים בפרויקטים של שיקום אקולוגי. מנגד, ממשלת בריטניה הגנה על הצעד וטענה כי הוא חיוני לעידוד בניית הדירות הנדרשת במדינה לצד השקעות ענק בשיקום הטבע.
